screens.title: Logical Backups with mysqldump
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why mysqldump is a foundational tool for logical backups and when to reach for it. Mysqldump exports schema and data as S Q L statements that are portable across servers, easy to version, and simple to inspect. You will see basic commands to back up a single database, multiple databases, or all databases, and you will practice restoring a dump with the mysql client. We will also explore key options that make dumps reliable for transactional tables and replication setups, such as single-transaction for InnoDB consistency, master-data to record binary log position, and flush-logs to rotate logs before capture. Along the way you will learn how to include routines, triggers, and events, how to handle schema-only or data-only exports, and how to avoid common mistakes like character set mismatches and missing privileges. By the end you will understand where mysqldump fits in a backup strategy, how to construct safe command lines, and how to verify a restoration. Think about a recent backup task you performed and how mysqldump could make that task more repeatable and transparent.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Options & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: This page focuses on the options you'll use to make dumps reliable and the common problems DBAs face. You will learn to use --master-data to capture binary log coordinates, which is essential for setting up replicas and performing point-in-time recovery. You will learn when to add --flush-logs so that the recorded coordinates align with a new binary log file. We will also cover how to include stored routines, triggers, and events with explicit flags, because mysqldump does not include them by default. Then we turn to operational pitfalls: mismatched character sets that corrupt text on restore, insufficient privileges that cause partial dumps, and unwieldy file sizes for very large databases. For each pitfall there is a practical countermeasure: set the client character set explicitly, grant the necessary dump privileges, and stream the dump through gzip to reduce size. Understanding these objectives helps you move from creating ad-hoc dumps to running safe, repeatable backup jobs.

keyIdea.text: Key options make dumps consistent and replication-ready; common mistakes are character sets, permissions, and huge files.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Options & Troubleshooting

Options and Troubleshooting

Practical flags and how to avoid common operational mistakes.

--master-data
Embeds binary log filename and position so you can resume replication or perform point-in-time recovery.
--flush-logs
Rotates binary logs before the dump so the recorded position is at the start of a new file.
--routines, --triggers, --events
Include stored procedures, triggers, and scheduled events; these are not dumped by default.
Common mistakes
Character set mismatches, insufficient privileges, and huge uncompressed files are frequent causes of backup failure.

screens.title: Basic mysqldump Commands
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the simplest mysqldump workflows and practice the exact commands you will use. Mysqldump produces S Q L statements that recreate tables and insert rows. A typical single-database backup uses the mysqldump command followed by the database name and output redirection to a file. For example, creating a file named mydatabase_backup. sql captures CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements for that database. When you need several databases, use the --databases flag and list each database name; mysqldump will include CREATE DATABASE and USE statements in the dump. To capture every user-created database on the server, use --all-databases. These differences matter because the presence or absence of CREATE DATABASE statements affects how you restore the file. A common misconception is thinking all dumps include database creation commands; they do not for a single database dump unless you specify --databases. Practical tip: never hardcode passwords on the command line. Instead, rely on prompt-based -p or a protected my. cnf for automation. Example scenario: you want to move dev schema to a new host; a single-database dump can be inspected, versioned, and restored on the target. Closing question: what would you inspect in a generated S Q L file to confirm it contains both structure and rows?

keyIdea.text: mysqldump dbname > file.sql for single DB; --databases lists multiple DBs; --all-databases exports all user DBs.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Basic mysqldump Commands
Command examples
mysqldump -u root -p mydatabase > mydatabase_backup.sql

mysqldump -u root -p --databases db1 db2 > multiple_databases_backup.sql

mysqldump -u root -p --all-databases > all_databases_backup.sql
Notes
  • Single database dumps do not include CREATE DATABASE unless you used --databases.
  • Verify the dump file size and sample the top to confirm CREATE TABLE statements exist.
Key Takeaway

Pick the right mode: single DB for portability, --databases for multiple DBs, --all-databases for full exports.

What to check in the dump
Presence of CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements
For --databases, check for CREATE DATABASE and USE statements
Inspect top of file for comments and metadata
Example scenario
You need to copy a development schema to another host. Run a single-database dump and restore on the target with the mysql client, then verify tables and sample rows.

screens.title: Restoring from a mysqldump File
screens.narratorSegment: Restoring is the complementary skill to dumping. The mysql client reads and executes S Q L from a dump file to recreate schema and data. If the dump contains CREATE DATABASE and USE statements, you run the client without supplying a target database and let the dump control selection. If your dump was a single-database export, provide the target database name on the restore command. A typical restore involves feeding the dump file into the mysql command and watching for errors or warnings. Always verify restoration by listing tables and selecting sample rows. A common misconception is expecting the restore to be instantaneous for large files; in practice restores take time proportional to file size and index rebuilds. When verifying, also check stored routines, triggers, and events if you included them. Example: you restored cohortia_app and then ran commands to show tables and to select from the orders table; you should also inspect the procedure list for get_user_orders. Final reflective question: after restoring, what three checks would you run to confirm a successful recovery? Restoring from a mysqldump File means use mysql client to execute the dump file; verify tables, data, and database objects after restoration.. In practical terms, practical restoration steps using the mysql client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Restoring Dumps
Restore commands (examples)
mysql -u root -p mydatabase < mydatabase_backup.sql

mysql -u root -p < all_databases_backup.sql
Verification checks
  • Show tables to confirm schema objects exist.
  • Select sample rows to confirm data integrity.
  • Show procedures and triggers to confirm routines and triggers were restored.
Common issues during restore
Character set mismatches can corrupt text on restore. Ensure client and server charsets match.
Missing CREATE DATABASE statements require you to create the database first or restore to an existing schema.
Large restores may need monitoring for long-running index creation and temporary disk usage.
Key Takeaway

Restoration is deterministic if the dump contains the required CREATE statements; always verify objects and sample data.

screens.title: --single-transaction Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding --single-transaction is central to producing consistent logical backups for transactional tables. The option begins a transaction before reading table data, which creates a consistent snapshot for engines that support MVCC, like InnoDB. Because InnoDB maintains multi-version data, the transaction sees a stable view even while other sessions continue to write. This prevents capturing rows from different points in time across tables or within a table, which can cause logical inconsistencies after restore. One important caveat is that --single-transaction does not prevent DDL operations or guarantee consistency for non-transactional engines like MyISAM; mysqldump briefly acquires a read lock for those during the dump. A common misconception is thinking --single-transaction locks tables for the entire dump; it does not lock InnoDB tables, which allows minimal disruption to the running application. Example: for a busy e-commerce site using InnoDB, run mysqldump with --single-transaction to avoid pause-inducing table locks while keeping a consistent snapshot. Closing question: what would you do differently if your server had many MyISAM tables? --single-transaction Explained means --single-transaction creates a transactional snapshot for innodb, avoiding long full-table locks and inconsistent snapshots.. In practical terms, how consistent snapshots work for innodb when using mysqldump. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › --single-transaction
Definition

--single-transaction starts a transaction at dump time, providing a stable snapshot for InnoDB's MVCC. It avoids prolonged locks and produces consistent output even with concurrent writes.

Use it for InnoDB tables to ensure a single point-in-time view.
Does not protect against DDL changes during the dump; DDL may still cause inconsistencies.
MyISAM tables require explicit locking because they are non-transactional.
Key Takeaway

Prefer --single-transaction for InnoDB to get a consistent snapshot without long read locks.

Concrete example
mysqldump -u backup -p --single-transaction mydatabase > consistent_backup.sql
Misconception: --single-transaction locks tables for the entire dump. Reality: it starts a transaction and avoids table locks for InnoDB; only brief locks may be used for non-transactional engines.

screens.title: --master-data and --flush-logs
screens.narratorSegment: --master-data records the binary log file name and position in the dump so you know exactly where to continue applying binary logs after a restore. This metadata is critical for setting up a replica or for point-in-time recovery, because it tells you where to start replaying events. The option may embed a CHANGE MASTER TO statement directly in the dump; you can choose to include it or comment it out with a numeric argument. Pairing --master-data with --flush-logs rotates the binary logs before the dump, ensuring that the recorded position corresponds to the start of a fresh log file. This simplifies later recovery because you can safely archive or ship the rotated log and know your starting point. A common mistake is not rotating logs, which can make it harder to locate the recorded coordinates among many existing log files. Example: when preparing a replica, include --master-data=2 so the position is recorded as a comment you can read without immediately applying it. Closing reflective question: how would you use the recorded position to start replication on a new replica? --master-data and --flush-logs means --master-data embeds binary log position information; --flush-logs rotates logs so the position is at a fresh file start.. In practical terms, why binary log coordinates and log rotation matter for replication and pitr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › --master-data & --flush-logs
What they do

--master-data inserts the binary log filename and position into the dump so you know where to resume binary log application. --flush-logs rotates binary logs before the dump, aligning the recorded position with a fresh log file.

Use --master-data=2 to record the position as a commented CHANGE MASTER TO line.
Pair with --flush-logs to simplify locating the recorded log file during recovery.
Misconception: skipping log rotation will still be fine. In reality, without rotation the recorded position may fall in the middle of a busy log file, making recovery ordering more complex.
Concrete example
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction --master-data=2 --flush-logs mydatabase > with_binlog_info.sql
Key Takeaway

Record binary log coordinates when preparing replication or point-in-time recovery, and rotate logs to simplify later log selection.

screens.title: Schema-only vs Data-only Dumps
screens.narratorSegment: Mysqldump provides fine-grained modes to export only structure or only data. The --no-data flag exports all CREATE statements but no INSERTs, giving you a schema-only file ideal for migrating table definitions or initializing an empty environment. The --no-create-info flag produces only INSERT statements without the CREATE TABLE text, which is useful when you're populating an existing schema. A common confusion is thinking these flags are default synonyms; they are opposite behaviors and must be chosen deliberately. An example use case: when deploying a schema change workflow, you might generate a schema-only dump to version control DDL, and separately produce a data-only dump for migrating reference data. When using --no-data for InnoDB, still consider --single-transaction to ensure any concurrent DDL or ephemeral changes do not leave the schema inconsistent. Closing question: in what scenario would you prefer separate schema-only and data-only dumps rather than a combined dump? Schema-only vs Data-only Dumps means --no-data exports structure only; --no-create-info exports data only. use them for separate schema/version workflows.. In practical terms, choosing between --no-data and --no-create-info. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Schema vs Data
Schema-only: --no-data
Exports CREATE TABLE, indexes, and constraints without any row data. Useful for versioning DDL or preparing empty schemas on new hosts.
mysqldump -u root -p --no-data mydatabase > schema_only.sql
Data-only: --no-create-info
Exports INSERT statements only. Use when the target schema already exists and you need to populate or migrate rows.
mysqldump -u root -p --no-create-info mydatabase > data_only.sql
Key Takeaway

Split schema and data when you need separate lifecycles for DDL and row data, or to reduce restore time for large datasets.

screens.title: Including Routines, Triggers, and Events
screens.narratorSegment: By default mysqldump does not include stored procedures, functions, triggers, or events, so you must request them explicitly. The flags --routines, --triggers, and --events add these objects to the dump. This is vital because application logic often lives in stored routines and triggers; omitting them leads to functional differences after restoration. A typical mistake is running a dump without these flags, restoring to a new server, and then discovering missing procedures that the application depends on. Example: if your cohortia_app depends on a get_user_orders procedure and an update_product_stock trigger, include --routines and --triggers to ensure they are re-created. Keep in mind that restoring routines may require appropriate DEFINER privileges or adjustments to user accounts. Practical tip: always inspect the dump file for CREATE PROCEDURE and CREATE TRIGGER statements to confirm inclusion. Closing question: what privileges or environment steps might be required to restore routines safely? Including Routines, Triggers, and Events means use --routines, --triggers, and --events to capture procedural and event objects; otherwise they will be missing after restore.. In practical terms, options to capture stored procedures, triggers, and scheduled events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Routines, Triggers, Events
Why include them?

Stored procedures, functions, triggers, and events may implement critical business logic. If they are not exported, a restored database will lack application behavior even if tables and data are present.

--routines includes CREATE PROCEDURE and CREATE FUNCTION statements.
--triggers includes CREATE TRIGGER statements for table-level triggers.
--events includes scheduled events defined in the database event scheduler.
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events mydatabase > full_schema_data.sql
Misconception: objects will be recreated automatically. Reality: you must include explicit flags and ensure the restore user has sufficient privileges.
Key Takeaway

Always include procedural and scheduled objects when they are part of application behavior; verify their CREATE statements in the dump.

screens.title: Permission and Privilege Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Mysqldump runs server-side SELECTs and metadata queries and therefore requires a set of privileges to produce complete backups. Typical minimum privileges include SELECT on the objects being dumped and SHOW VIEW if views are present. If you use --flush-logs, additional privileges such as RELOAD are required because the server must rotate logs. For capturing binary log coordinates with --master-data or to read global status you might need REPLICATION CLIENT. Missing privileges result in partial dumps or errors that silently omit objects. A common mistake is running automated backups under a user with only SELECT; the dump may fail to include triggers, routines, or rotated logs. Best practice: grant a dedicated backup user the minimal required set of privileges, limit its scope to the necessary databases, and store credentials securely. Example: a backup user with SELECT, SHOW VIEW, PROCESS, RELOAD, and REPLICATION CLIENT privileges will handle most dump modes. Closing question: how would you audit a dump to detect missing objects caused by insufficient privileges? Permission and Privilege Requirements means ensure the backup user has select, show view, process, reload, and replication client as needed to produce complete dumps.. In practical terms, what the dumping user must be allowed to do. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Permissions & Privileges
Minimum privileges
  • SELECT on exported objects
  • SHOW VIEW to dump views
  • PROCESS for some status reads
  • RELOAD for --flush-logs
  • REPLICATION CLIENT for --master-data
Misconception: using root is required. In practice, a dedicated backup user with narrowly scoped privileges is safer and sufficient when configured correctly.
Practical safeguard
Create a dedicated backup user, grant only the needed privileges, and store credentials in a secured my.cnf file with restricted file permissions.
Key Takeaway

A properly-privileged backup user prevents silent omissions and supports automation without exposing full administrative credentials.

screens.title: Handling Character Sets and Encoding
screens.narratorSegment: Character set mismatches are a frequent cause of corrupted text after a dump and restore. Mysqldump uses the client character set when producing S Q L. If your database uses utf8mb4 but the mysqldump client defaults to latin1, the exported bytes may not match expectations and restoring those bytes will produce invalid or mangled text. The practical countermeasure is to set the client character set explicitly with the --default-character-set option on both dump and restore commands, or ensure the client environment matches server settings. Always inspect text-heavy tables after a restore for multi-byte characters to catch problems early. A common misconception is thinking dumps are automatically character-set safe; they are not. Example: include --default-character-set=utf8mb4 in both the dump and restore steps to preserve emoji and multi-byte content. Closing question: after restoring, what simple query would you run to validate multi-byte text integrity? Handling Character Sets and Encoding means specify --default-character-set to ensure the dump preserves multi-byte characters and avoids corruption on restore.. In practical terms, avoid corrupted text by matching client and server character sets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Character Sets
Problem

If mysqldump and mysql use different character sets than the server, exported or restored text can be corrupted, especially for multi-byte characters like emoji.

Solution: use --default-character-set=utf8mb4 consistently on both dump and restore, or ensure your client environment matches the server charset.
Example commands
mysqldump -u root -p --default-character-set=utf8mb4 mydatabase > dump.sql mysql -u root -p --default-character-set=utf8mb4 mydatabase < dump.sql
Misconception: exporting text is safe without specifying charset. Always be explicit when multi-byte text exists.
Key Takeaway

Set and verify character sets for both dump and restore to protect multi-byte content integrity.

screens.title: Large Files, Compression, and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Large databases can produce very large S Q L files that are difficult to transfer and restore. Compressing the dump on the fly with a stream compressor reduces storage and network transfer costs; piping mysqldump into gzip is a common approach. Restoration can similarly stream through decompression before feeding into the mysql client. For very large datasets, logical backups may also be slower to restore than physical backups, since an S Q L import must recreate indexes and execute many statements. Consider compressing with gzip or similar tools to reduce footprint. Another performance consideration is using parallel export tools or partitioned exports for extremely large tables, but these approaches are beyond mysqldump's basic model. A common misconception is expecting compressed dumps to restore instantly; decompression and import still take time. Example: mysqldump piped to gzip produces a. sql. gz file that you can transfer and restore by piping through gunzip into mysql. Closing question: what tradeoffs do you accept when you choose logical backups with compression over a physical snapshot? Large Files, Compression, and Performance means pipe mysqldump to gzip for smaller files; restoration still requires decompression and import time, and very large dbs may favor physical backups.. content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Large Files & Compression
Compression pattern
mysqldump -u root -p mydatabase | gzip > backup.sql.gz gunzip < backup.sql.gz | mysql -u root -p mydatabase
Benefits: smaller storage and network use. Tradeoff: CPU for compression and additional time for decompression during restore.
Performance considerations
  • Logical restores rebuild indexes and replay many statements, which can be slow.
  • Physical backups are faster to restore for very large data volumes.
Key Takeaway

Compress dumps to save space; accept decompression and import time. For massive data sets, evaluate physical backups.

Starter commands and hints

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why mysqldump is a foundational tool for logical backups and when to reach for it. Mysqldump exports schema and data as S Q L statements that are portable across servers, easy to version, and simple to inspect. You will see basic commands to back up a single database, multiple databases, or all databases, and you will practice restoring a dump with the mysql client. We will also explore key options that make dumps reliable for transactional tables and replication setups, such as single-transaction for InnoDB consistency, master-data to record binary log position, and flush-logs to rotate logs before capture. Along the way you will learn how to include routines, triggers, and events, how to handle schema-only or data-only exports, and how to avoid common mistakes like character set mismatches and missing privileges. By the end you will understand where mysqldump fits in a backup strategy, how to construct safe command lines, and how to verify a restoration. Think about a recent backup task you performed and how mysqldump could make that task more repeatable and transparent.

By the end of this chapter you will execute mysqldump commands to create full and selective backups, and you will restore those backups using the mysql client. You will learn how to craft dumps for single databases, multiple databases, and complete server exports. You will also understand how to include or exclude schema and data, and how to add routines, triggers, and events to a dump. Moreover, you will become familiar with options that ensure consistency for transactional engines and options that make dumps replication-ready. Each objective builds a practical skill: creating a reliable dump, selecting what to include, restoring without surprises, and avoiding common operational mistakes. These skills matter because they let you create reproducible backups, recover from failures, and set up replicas from a known binary log position. Think of these objectives as verified milestones toward daily DBA tasks: a backup you can inspect, a restore you can trust, and a command you can automate safely.

This page focuses on the options you'll use to make dumps reliable and the common problems DBAs face. You will learn to use --master-data to capture binary log coordinates, which is essential for setting up replicas and performing point-in-time recovery. You will learn when to add --flush-logs so that the recorded coordinates align with a new binary log file. We will also cover how to include stored routines, triggers, and events with explicit flags, because mysqldump does not include them by default. Then we turn to operational pitfalls: mismatched character sets that corrupt text on restore, insufficient privileges that cause partial dumps, and unwieldy file sizes for very large databases. For each pitfall there is a practical countermeasure: set the client character set explicitly, grant the necessary dump privileges, and stream the dump through gzip to reduce size. Understanding these objectives helps you move from creating ad-hoc dumps to running safe, repeatable backup jobs.

Let's define the simplest mysqldump workflows and practice the exact commands you will use. Mysqldump produces S Q L statements that recreate tables and insert rows. A typical single-database backup uses the mysqldump command followed by the database name and output redirection to a file. For example, creating a file named mydatabase_backup. sql captures CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements for that database. When you need several databases, use the --databases flag and list each database name; mysqldump will include CREATE DATABASE and USE statements in the dump. To capture every user-created database on the server, use --all-databases. These differences matter because the presence or absence of CREATE DATABASE statements affects how you restore the file. A common misconception is thinking all dumps include database creation commands; they do not for a single database dump unless you specify --databases. Practical tip: never hardcode passwords on the command line. Instead, rely on prompt-based -p or a protected my. cnf for automation. Example scenario: you want to move dev schema to a new host; a single-database dump can be inspected, versioned, and restored on the target. Closing question: what would you inspect in a generated S Q L file to confirm it contains both structure and rows?

Restoring is the complementary skill to dumping. The mysql client reads and executes S Q L from a dump file to recreate schema and data. If the dump contains CREATE DATABASE and USE statements, you run the client without supplying a target database and let the dump control selection. If your dump was a single-database export, provide the target database name on the restore command. A typical restore involves feeding the dump file into the mysql command and watching for errors or warnings. Always verify restoration by listing tables and selecting sample rows. A common misconception is expecting the restore to be instantaneous for large files; in practice restores take time proportional to file size and index rebuilds. When verifying, also check stored routines, triggers, and events if you included them. Example: you restored cohortia_app and then ran commands to show tables and to select from the orders table; you should also inspect the procedure list for get_user_orders. Final reflective question: after restoring, what three checks would you run to confirm a successful recovery? Restoring from a mysqldump File means use mysql client to execute the dump file; verify tables, data, and database objects after restoration.. In practical terms, practical restoration steps using the mysql client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding --single-transaction is central to producing consistent logical backups for transactional tables. The option begins a transaction before reading table data, which creates a consistent snapshot for engines that support MVCC, like InnoDB. Because InnoDB maintains multi-version data, the transaction sees a stable view even while other sessions continue to write. This prevents capturing rows from different points in time across tables or within a table, which can cause logical inconsistencies after restore. One important caveat is that --single-transaction does not prevent DDL operations or guarantee consistency for non-transactional engines like MyISAM; mysqldump briefly acquires a read lock for those during the dump. A common misconception is thinking --single-transaction locks tables for the entire dump; it does not lock InnoDB tables, which allows minimal disruption to the running application. Example: for a busy e-commerce site using InnoDB, run mysqldump with --single-transaction to avoid pause-inducing table locks while keeping a consistent snapshot. Closing question: what would you do differently if your server had many MyISAM tables? --single-transaction Explained means --single-transaction creates a transactional snapshot for innodb, avoiding long full-table locks and inconsistent snapshots.. In practical terms, how consistent snapshots work for innodb when using mysqldump. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. --master-data records the binary log file name and position in the dump so you know exactly where to continue applying binary logs after a restore. This metadata is critical for setting up a replica or for point-in-time recovery, because it tells you where to start replaying events. The option may embed a CHANGE MASTER TO statement directly in the dump; you can choose to include it or comment it out with a numeric argument. Pairing --master-data with --flush-logs rotates the binary logs before the dump, ensuring that the recorded position corresponds to the start of a fresh log file. This simplifies later recovery because you can safely archive or ship the rotated log and know your starting point. A common mistake is not rotating logs, which can make it harder to locate the recorded coordinates among many existing log files. Mysqldump provides fine-grained modes to export only structure or only data. The --no-data flag exports all CREATE statements but no INSERTs, giving you a schema-only file ideal for migrating table definitions or initializing an empty environment. The --no-create-info flag produces only INSERT statements without the CREATE TABLE text, which is useful when you're populating an existing schema. A common confusion is thinking these flags are default synonyms; they are opposite behaviors and must be chosen deliberately. Mysqldump runs server-side SELECTs and metadata queries and therefore requires a set of privileges to produce complete backups. Character set mismatches are a frequent cause of corrupted text after a dump and restore. Mysqldump uses the client character set when producing S Q L. If your database uses utf8mb4 but the mysqldump client defaults to latin1, the exported bytes may not match expectations and restoring those bytes will produce invalid or mangled text. The practical countermeasure is to set the client character set explicitly with the --default-character-set option on both dump and restore commands, or ensure the client environment matches server settings. Always inspect text-heavy tables after a restore for multi-byte characters to catch problems early. A common misconception is thinking dumps are automatically character-set safe; they are not. Large databases can produce very large S Q L files that are difficult to transfer and restore. Compressing the dump on the fly with a stream compressor reduces storage and network transfer costs; piping mysqldump into gzip is a common approach. Restoration can similarly stream through decompression before feeding into the mysql client. For very large datasets, logical backups may also be slower to restore than physical backups, since an S Q L import must recreate indexes and execute many statements. Consider compressing with gzip or similar tools to reduce footprint. Another performance consideration is using parallel export tools or partitioned exports for extremely large tables, but these approaches are beyond mysqldump's basic model. A common misconception is expecting compressed dumps to restore instantly; decompression and import still take time.
